title: The priestly blessing (Numbers 6:24–26)
hook: the Lord bless you and keep you, make his face shine on you
carry: the lord bless you and keep you

segments.voice: Yesterday, the jubilee: a ram's horn, land returned, people sent home free. Your line was proclaim liberty. Did you cancel a small debt? Day four hundred three.

In 1979, archaeologists digging in old burial caves just outside Jerusalem found two tiny rolled-up scrolls of silver, each small enough to hide in your palm. They were so fragile it took years to unroll them. When they finally did, scratched into the silver were a few lines of Hebrew, among the oldest pieces of biblical text ever found, centuries older than the Dead Sea Scrolls. Someone had worn them, probably as amulets, maybe around the neck. And the words inside were a blessing. The same blessing many churches send people home with every Sunday. Today, three lines that people have been carrying close for more than two and a half thousand years.
screen: `TWO SILVER SCROLLS IN A TOMB.` → `OLDER THAN THE DEAD SEA SCROLLS.` → `THE WORDS INSIDE: A BLESSING.`

segments.voice: In the book of Numbers, God tells Moses to tell Aaron and his sons, the priests: this is how you shall bless the people. And then the words, in the King James Bible: "The LORD bless thee, and keep thee: The LORD make his face shine upon thee, and be gracious unto thee: The LORD lift up his countenance upon thee, and give thee peace." Three lines. And they grow. In Hebrew, the first line is three words, the second five, the third seven. Like a wave building. Each line names the LORD, and then gives two gifts. Bless and keep: provide for you and guard you. Shine and be gracious: the picture is a face lighting up when it sees you, the way a grandparent's face does when you walk in. Lift up his countenance: turn toward you, look right at you. And the last word, the one everything has been building to, is shalom: peace, wholeness, nothing missing. Notice too that it's thee, singular. In Hebrew, the blessing is spoken to the whole people, but every you is a single you. A crowd is blessed, one person at a time. Then God says why: "they shall put my name upon the children of Israel; and I will bless them." The priests speak the words. God does the blessing. In synagogues, it's still said by descendants of the priests, the kohanim. In churches it's used everywhere: Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant pastors raise their hands and say it at the end of services, at weddings, over newborns, at graves.
screen: `THREE LINES: THREE, FIVE, SEVEN WORDS.` · `A FACE THAT LIGHTS UP.` · `ENDING IN SHALOM.` · `PRIESTS SPEAK, GOD BLESSES.` · then, large: `THE LORD MAKE HIS FACE SHINE UPON THEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say the blessing over someone. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person: someone you love, someone you're worried about, or someone you find difficult. See their face. Then, quietly, aloud or inside, say the old words over them, slowly, one line per breath. The LORD bless thee, and keep thee. The LORD make his face shine upon thee, and be gracious unto thee. The LORD lift up his countenance upon thee, and give thee peace. If those words aren't yours to say, simply hold them in mind and wish them well. The bell holds the time.
The priestly blessing. Three lines from Numbers six, given to Aaron's priests, still said in synagogues and churches, and found on silver scrolls in a Jerusalem tomb.
Your line: the lord bless you and keep you. Today, say it, or think it, over one person as they leave the room. Day four hundred three.

howItsDone: Many pastors and priests say the Aaronic blessing at the end of worship with raised hands, and it is often spoken at weddings, baptisms and funerals; in synagogues, the kohanim say it over the congregation.

original.note: Hebrew: may he bless you, the first word of the blessing.

trapdoor: what you thought: the nice thing the pastor says at the end.
what it means: a blessing God gave the priests to speak, growing line by line toward peace, spoken to each person as a single you.
what a scholar hears: three, five, seven Hebrew words; and the Ketef Hinnom silver scrolls, among the oldest known biblical text, carry a form of it.

notes: Ketef Hinnom scrolls: found 1979 by Gabriel Barkay; dated to the late seventh or early sixth century BC; unrolled and read over following years. The script says 'more than two and a half thousand years'. Confirm.
Word counts 3/5/7 in the Hebrew of 6:24–26 (counting YHWH as a word); confirm.
Original: יְבָרֶכְךָ is the first word of the blessing (before YHWH); confirm. Pronunciation 'ye-va-re-KHE-kha'; check stress.
